title: Counting the Same Thing Everywhere: Data Platforms, Definitions and Analytics
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/28-commerce-data-and-analytics/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have: the carry-over from the previous chapter in p02, the thesis sentence in p03, a roadmap p05, a lead sentence for the failure table p50, a conclusion paragraph that answers the opening p51, and Part VI's closing (p56, p57) with a hand-off p58 rewritten to Part VII's question; see decision_log.

know: The difference between operational and analytical data, the warehouse or lakehouse, and the three ways data reaches it (scheduled extract-and-load, event streams, platform exports).

How public definitions of an order or of sales differ (Shopify's sales schema and annual report, Zalando's annual report, Google Analytics 4's purchase event), what a metric definition must settle, and what a metrics layer is.

The four uses of commerce data (reporting, experimentation, data science, merchandising and inventory planning), data products for partners, and the rule that separates live operational signals from business metrics shown on a lag.
believe: Three honest systems give three honest counts; none is the company's number until someone owns its definition.
Define before you build: written definitions with an owner do more for trust than a new warehouse or dashboard.
The number that gets believed is the number published with its bridge to each system's count.
can_do: Attribute each difference between two counts to definition, collection or time.
Write a definition table for order, net sales and return that settles cancellations, exchanges, test orders, split shipments, store transactions, dates and tax.
Decide which numbers to show live and which on a lag, and whether to feed the warehouse by extract-and-load or by events.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the analyst or data engineer who inherits a warehouse without definitions, and next the product manager or finance partner who has to defend a number; the engineering lead gets the design choices by stage.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what a database, a report and a dashboard are.

Kestrel & Pine, its people (Mara Lindqvist, Milan Petrov, Sanne de Wit, Daniel Okafor, Hanna Berg, Teun Baas), its thirteen systems and 34 integrations, its incidents in outline and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' and 'commerce platform', business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

Parts II to V: one owner per product, price and stock fact; available-to-promise; checkout creating the order once; refunds as new payments; one order record with three status lines; one invoice per shipment, credit notes and the monthly match; marketplace orders reaching the ERP as a weekly summary and store sales as a nightly total.

Part VI so far: integration styles and the integration inventory with an owner per flow; events, idempotency keys and the reconciliation sweep; contracts, pinned versions, sunset dates and rate budgets; a master per entity, the cross-reference with its merge log, and automatic links only on exact keys.
does_not_know: Operational and analytical data; data warehouse; lakehouse; business intelligence (BI) tool.
Extract-and-load (ELT), a lookback window, event streams as a feed for analytics, platform bulk exports.
Metric definition, metrics layer (semantic layer), GMV, VAT-inclusive and exclusive bases, IFRS 15 recognition.
Sell-through, weeks of cover, data product, data mesh, operational signal versus business metric, the bridge between counts.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three order counts from three systems, the reader explains them by definition, collection and time and says what the company should report, rather than picking one system as right.
acceptance_criteria.probe: For one month a brand's storefront reports 21,050 orders, its ERP 22,710 and its warehouse report 24,140. The storefront counts orders created, including canceled, test and exchange orders and no marketplace orders; the ERP counts sales orders invoiced, with marketplace orders from a weekly summary; the warehouse report counts parcels shipped. Using only this chapter: which count is right, and what should the company report?
acceptance_criteria.expected: None is wrong: they differ by definition (cancellations, test orders, exchanges, parcels against orders, store receipts), by collection (marketplace orders absent from the platform and summarized weekly in the ERP) and by time (creation, invoice and ship dates). An owner, such as the Data Lead, writes one definition (an order counted at confirmation in every channel including marketplace-fulfilled ones, test orders excluded, cancellations counted with their status, an exchange not an order, a split order one order) and publishes the company's count with the bridge to each system's count; a difference the bridge does not explain is an exception to investigate.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a live count and a later report differ and how each should be shown.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A live dashboard showed 2,300 orders in the peak hour; the report a week later says 2,210. Using only this chapter: which is wrong, and how should the two numbers be shown?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Neither: the live count was taken before cancellations, refunds, edits and duplicates arrived. Operational signals (orders per minute, error rates, queue depth, integration lag) are shown live and approximate for acting now; business metrics are shown on a lag with a definition, a revision policy and the reconciliation beside them, and the two are not given the same label.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say when to feed the analytical store by extract-and-load and when by events.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: should a merchant feed its data warehouse by scheduled extract-and-load from its platform or by event streams?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Extract-and-load with a lookback window until the operational systems emit events; once an OMS and an availability service publish order and stock events, the warehouse reads the same stream. Incremental extraction is a sweep, so a late edit it misses stays a difference until a comparison finds it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why finance and operations can bring different correct order totals and how that misleads decisions; that the storefront, the ERP and the warehouse count different things and should sometimes differ; that analytics must separate differences that follow from definitions from missing or wrong data; W7 giving the Data Lead the definitions of order, revenue and return, settled before dashboards; Eva's order becoming an order, invoice lines and a parcel, and her exchange a credit note and a second parcel. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's three February counts and published metric definitions.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

The conclusion performs Part VI's closing: it sets the part's five cases against the part opening's order that reaches the warehouse twice, stock update that arrives after the last unit has sold and invoice whose customer finance cannot identify, and states what the cases have in common, rather than only listing the part's questions.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does the conclusion return to Part VI's opening failures (an order reaching the warehouse twice, a stock update arriving after the last unit sold, an invoice naming a customer finance cannot identify) and say what the part's five cases have in common?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Yes: it names the part's cases (the Black Friday stock chain, the Double Refund, the Deprecated Endpoint, Eva's four records, February's three counts), says that in each both ends worked and something about the join had not been decided, and names the remedy as a record with an owner, not a new system.

thesis.question: Why do three reports show three different order counts, and how do you build analytics that the business trusts?
thesis.claim: Each system counts what it exists to handle (orders created, sales orders invoiced, parcels shipped), from the records that reach it, dated by its own clock, so correct counts differ by definition, collection and time. Analytics are trusted when every system's data is copied into one analytical store, each metric is defined once with an owner, and the company's number is published with a bridge reconciling it to each system's count.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that one of the counts is right and the others are errors, so the fix is to name a system of record for orders or build a real-time dashboard, and that a data warehouse and a BI tool by themselves give the business one number.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim writes definitions with owners before it adds dashboards, and treats a difference the bridge does not explain as an incident. For February 2027 Kestrel & Pine's platform counted 21,050 orders, its ERP 22,710 and its warehouse report 24,140, and in March nobody owned the definition. Under W7 the Data Lead, Hanna Berg, published definitions in June 2027, adopted from the July close: February became 23,150 orders, 22,860 net of cancellations, with 9,200 store transactions reported beside them. The bridge found its first unexplained exception in August 2027, 23 marketplace orders dropped from the connector's weekly summary during a vendor outage. The definitions took three weeks; the warehouse already existed.
thesis.how_why: An operational system stores what its job needs, one record at a time, and dates each record by the moment of that job: creation, invoice or shipment. Copies reach the analytical store by extract jobs with lookback windows or by events, and a late edit missed by both stays a difference until something compares them. Every dashboard that computes 'order' for itself decides cancellations, exchanges, test orders, split shipments and dates again; a definition kept as code in one place, with an owner, takes those choices out of the dashboards, and the bridge sorts each remaining difference into an explained definition or a missing record.

supporting_claims.claim: Each operational system counts what it exists to handle, from the records that reach it, on its own clock, so honest counts differ by definition, collection and time, and none is the company's number until someone owns the definition.

Operational and analytical work need separate stores, and every system's data is copied into one analytical store by extract-and-load, event streams or platform exports; incremental extraction is a sweep, so a late edit it misses stays a difference until a comparison finds it.

A metric definition settles what is counted, which records are in or out, which date and tax basis apply and how later changes are reported; public definitions differ, so each metric is defined once, as code in a metrics layer, with a named owner, and every use of the data (reporting, experimentation, data science, planning, partner data products) computes from it.

Live operational signals and business metrics are different objects: signals are shown live and approximate for acting now, metrics on a lag with a definition, a revision policy and the reconciliation beside them, never under one label.

The design follows the stage: platform reports at Starting, a warehouse fed by extract-and-load with a metrics layer at Omnichannel, an event stream and lakehouse at Group; at every stage the definitions and their owner matter more than the tool.

The company's number is published with a bridge to each system's count; the bridge sorts every difference into an explained definition or a missing record, and an unexplained difference is an exception to investigate.

role.contribution: Gives the part its last join, between the operational systems and the numbers the business decides by: copies of every system in one analytical store, one owned definition per metric, and the bridge to each system's count; performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with a one-sentence list of the part's questions and the hand-off to Part VII).

additional_patterns.applies_to: opanalytical to realtime: the analytical store, the ways data reaches it, the definitions and bridge computed in it, the uses that depend on them, and the freshness each needs with the live view that sits outside them

flow.rationale: The three February counts come first because every later section answers part of the question they raise: why the counts differ and what the company should report. The analytical store comes next because definitions, uses and the bridge all need one place where every system's data is copied; the three ways of getting data there follow, since each explains how a record can be missed on the way (a collection difference in the scene). Definitions, the metrics layer and the bridge come after the store they are computed in and before the uses, because every use depends on shared definitions. The freshness table and real-time dashboards follow the uses because the table compares the uses with the live view, the one view that is not computed from settled definitions. The four designs and the stage table compare the options once the reader has all the parts, including the bridge the recommendation adds; W7 in practice then resolves the scene's three counts with a definition table and a bridge; the failures come last because each is read against a part of the design. Putting the definitions before the store would leave the reader asking where a definition is computed; putting the freshness table before the uses would refer to uses not yet named; putting W7 before the definitions would show the answer before the reader knows what a definition must settle.

sections.heading: Operational Data and Analytical Data
sections.controlling_idea: The same facts are used one record at a time to run the business and across all records to analyse it, the two uses need separate stores, and one analytical store (a warehouse or a lakehouse) must receive every system's data.

advances_thesis.how: Establishes the one place where the counts can be compared.

flow.rationale: The distinction first, then why the stores must be apart, then the two forms of the analytical store, then the judgement that for this merchant the form is a vendor choice.

transition_in.carries_over: Counts that can only be compared somewhere all of them land.
transition_in.introduces: The two uses of the same facts and the store each needs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three counts can only be compared where all of them land, and the first idea a newcomer needs is that the same facts are used in two different ways that want different stores.

Operational data is the live state of the business, read and written one record at a time and fast; analytical data is the history laid out for questions across all records, which read millions of rows and tolerate hours of lag.

transition_in.carries_over: Two ways of using the same facts.
transition_in.introduces: Each way defined, with examples.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two must be kept apart because an analytical query competes with checkout for the same machine, so analytical questions never run against an operational store and an analytical store is never trusted for an operational answer.

evidence.what: A year-long report run against the platform's database on a Friday evening in November; 'the dashboard says it shipped' is not a shipment.
evidence.shows: Mixing the two uses slows checkout one way and misleads operations the other.

transition_in.introduces: Why they need separate stores, and the rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The analytical store comes in two forms; the first, a data warehouse, is a database built for large analytical queries into which copies of every system's data are loaded and modelled, and vendors describe separating storage from compute so one team's queries do not slow another's.

sections.heading: What the Data Is For
sections.controlling_idea: Every use of the data computes from the shared definitions: the same warehouse serves reporting, experimentation, data science, merchandising and inventory planning, and partners, each with different tolerances.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that every use of the data depends on the definitions and says who owns them.

flow.rationale: The uses in turn, internal first and partners last; partners come last because their data products add a contract and consent to the definitions the internal uses share.

transition_in.carries_over: One owned definition per metric, published with its bridge.
transition_in.introduces: The uses that compute from it and their different tolerances.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every use of the data inherits the definitions and their bridge, and the same warehouse serves four internal audiences with different tolerances, and partners from the Omnichannel stage, which a design should name.
Reporting is the monthly and weekly record, and it must be defined, reconciled and revised with a stated policy.

transition_in.carries_over: Four audiences.
transition_in.introduces: The first, reporting.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Experimentation compares two versions on randomly split traffic and needs event-level data with a stable key and the same metric definitions as reporting.

transition_in.carries_over: Reporting's definitions.
transition_in.introduces: Experimentation, which must use the same definitions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Data science builds forecasts and models from the modelled tables and writes back predictions, and it is the main reason to keep raw history.

transition_in.carries_over: Experimentation.
transition_in.introduces: Data science.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Merchandising and inventory planning is the most commercially important use at Kestrel & Pine's stage, and its two numbers, sell-through and weeks of cover, depend on one definition of a sale and one view of stock.

evidence.what: Teun Baas reading sell-through on the moss Ridgewalker; Daniel Okafor reading weeks of cover; stock across Duiven, six stores and the marketplace program's location.
evidence.shows: Planning numbers inherit the definition of a sale and the inventory work of W1.

transition_in.carries_over: Data science.
transition_in.introduces: Merchandising and inventory planning, the use that matters most here.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Data products for partners appear at the Omnichannel stage; warehouses now make delivery cheap, which moves the cost to definitions and consent.

evidence.what: Snowflake's Secure Data Sharing with 'no actual data ... copied'; Databricks' open sharing protocol across platforms.
evidence.shows: Delivery is cheap; a sell-through feed is still a disclosure and a customer-level feed is personal data.
evidence.source: Snowflake and Databricks documentation, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The internal uses.
transition_in.introduces: Uses outside the company: data products for partners.

sections.heading: Real-Time Dashboards and When They Mislead
sections.controlling_idea: Each flow of data needs its own freshness and completeness, and a live dashboard counts while records are still arriving, so live operational signals and business metrics shown on a lag with a definition, a revision policy and the reconciliation are different objects and must not share a label.

advances_thesis.how: Explains the time cause of differences for live views and gives the rule for showing each kind of number.

transition_in.carries_over: Uses that compute from shared definitions on settled data.
transition_in.introduces: How fresh each flow must be, and the live view that counts before the data has settled.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The uses work on settled data while running the business live does not, so each flow of data (orders and shipments, stock snapshots, finance figures, operational dashboards, board reports) needs its own freshness and completeness, with a different system allowed to disagree.

evidence.what: Five flows (orders and shipments, stock snapshots, finance figures, operational dashboards, board reports) with how fresh, how complete, who may disagree and the typical mechanism; illustrative targets.
evidence.shows: The mechanism follows the flow's needs; finance must reconcile to the cent while an orders-per-minute view can be approximate.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table's last two rows, a live orders-per-minute dashboard and a monthly order count, are the ones that get confused, and showing both under one label makes the dashboard a fourth opinion.

transition_in.carries_over: The table's last two rows, live operational dashboards and monthly board reports.
transition_in.introduces: The confusion between a rate and a record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A real-time dashboard counts while orders, refunds and payment records are still arriving, so a live view and a closed-period report can disagree without either calculation being wrong.

evidence.what: GA4's intraday export is best-effort and some attribution lags up to 24 hours; Stripe: a payout 'might arrive before its reconciliation data is ready'.
evidence.shows: The vendors document the delays that make a live count provisional.
evidence.source: Google Analytics, Stripe and Shopify documentation, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: A rate for acting now against a record that will be revised.
transition_in.introduces: Why a live count is provisional: records are still arriving, as the vendors document.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Operational signals are rates for acting in the next ten minutes and are shown live and approximate; business metrics are records shown on a lag with a definition, a revision policy and the reconciliation beside them.

evidence.what: A live 2,300 orders against a reported 2,210, with 90 canceled, refunded, edited or duplicated after the dashboard counted them; Figure 3.
evidence.shows: Mixing the two under one label produces a question with a predictable answer.

transition_in.carries_over: A live view and a report that disagree.
transition_in.introduces: The rule that separates the two kinds of number.

flow.rationale: The freshness table first, because it sets the live operational view beside the settled reports; then the confusion between its last two rows, the reason a live count is provisional, and the rule that separates them. The table needs the uses of the previous section, which is why it sits here rather than with the mechanisms; the rule needs the confusion stated first.

sections.heading: The Choices and Their Trade-offs

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Each failure of analytics comes from a missing part of the design (a missed late edit, two clocks, refunds netted on one side, reports on operational stores, browser analytics as the order count, a metric redefined in a dashboard, the warehouse used as a system of record, a partner feed without a contract), and each has a way to notice it and a fix.

advances_thesis.how: Shows each part of the design by what happens without it.

transition_in.carries_over: The design working at Kestrel & Pine.
transition_in.introduces: What goes wrong when a part of it is missing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most failures in analytics come from a part of the design that is missing, and each shows itself in a recognizable way.

evidence.what: Eight failures with how you notice each and what to do.
evidence.shows: Each part of the design, read by what happens without it.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The opening's meeting, where finance and operations bring different correct totals, is answered by the chapter's parts together: the counts differ by definition, collection and time; one analytical store receiving every system makes them comparable, one owned definition makes one of them the company's, and the bridge to each system's count turns every remaining difference into either an explained definition or a missing record. For the part: the Black Friday stock chain, the Double Refund, the Deprecated Endpoint, Eva's four records and February's three counts look like five problems in five technologies and are one: in each, both ends worked and something about the join had not been decided, and each chapter's remedy is a record with an owner.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can explain any two counts by definition, collection and time and write the definition before buying a dashboard; at Kestrel & Pine W7 took three weeks. Across Part VI the remedies were records with owners: W5's integration standards, Eva's four records made one master with three links in July 2027, and February restated as 23,150 orders with a bridge.

callback.to: The introduction's meeting where finance and operations bring different correct totals; and, for the part, the Part VI opening's order that reaches the warehouse twice, stock update that arrives after the last unit has sold and invoice whose customer finance cannot identify.
callback.how: p51 answers the chapter's opening meeting; p56 returns to the part opening and names what its five cases have in common; p57 gives the part's so-what and take-away.

takeaway.content: Write the definition of an order, net sales and return with an owner and publish the bridge to each system's count every month; for the part, build the integration inventory for your own landscape, one row per flow with its owner, idempotency key, pinned version and sunset date and reconciliation job, then name a master per shared entity and an owner per metric, starting with the rows that have no owner and the flows that move stock, orders or money with nothing comparing their two ends.
